newsitem.title: UK: North Korea at crisis point - UNICEF.
newsitem.headline: North Korea at crisis point - UNICEF.

text.p: North Korea is teetering on the edge of "a major humanitarian crisis" and needs outside help within weeks, a top United Nations official said on Thursday.
Peter McDermott, UNICEF's deputy director of emergency programmes, said all the signs of a crisis were in place -- only the scale of the potential disaster remained unclear.

"We have reached the critical juncture," McDermott told Reuters hours after returning from a 10-day trip to North Korea. "Even under the most optimistic scenario, there's going to be a major food problem."
The United Nations Children's Fund is one of the few organisations allowed access to remote North Korea, gripped by famine since devastating floods in 1995 and 1996.
McDermott said North Korea was now at its lowest ebb since the floods and the crisis was set to worsen by month's end.
The government is distributing 100 grammes -- a handful of rice -- to its citizens each day, but even that paltry ration will run out on June 20 as food and fuel dry up, he said.
"The big question is what happens after that," McDermott said. "The situation is critical and deteriorating fast but if we act now, we can prevent some of the worst effects."
The United Nations launched an appeal for more than $200 million just 10 weeks ago but McDermott said more money was already needed.
In the short term, he said, more and more of Korea's 2.6 million young children were at risk of dying, most from diseases linked to malnutrition.
As for the mid-term: "If the crop in September-October is not good, I suspect we will see by the end of the year a major humanitarian crisis."
Aside from massive food shortages, the health care system is "on the verge of collapse", fuel is very scarce and infrastructure is breaking down.
Children are growing up stunted by chronic hunger, three-year-olds cannot walk, rickets is on the rise and scabies is spreading, he said.
At one orphanage he visited, McDermott said 60 children out of 270 had died in the past year.
"Ten years ago, North Korea has some of the best indicators globally for child care but the floods exacerbated underlying problems and we're now seeing a downward acceleration," he said.
But fresh aid could be hard to drum up, with the international community divided over helping a hard-line communist country that craves isolation and is still technically at war with South Korea.
McDermott conceded fresh aid was not a given but said North Korea was trying hard to cooperate with outsiders and that he had seen no evidence of food being siphoned off by the powerful military.
"The government itself is having difficulty," he said. "They are not used to massive contact with the outside world and this is a major challenge to their philosophy of self-reliance."
